newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine growth should last after him.
newsitem.headline: Philippine growth should last after him.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday that no one in his right mind who was aspiring to succeed him would change his economic policies and risk plunging the Philippines back into a "black pit of economic depression."
He said the liberalisation measures had enabled the country to erase its image as the sick man of Asia. "We are now a young bull," he said.

"That's the best assurance that I can give you," he said when asked at his weekly news conference what guarantee investors had that the country would not lapse into a boom-and-bust cycle after his current six-year term ends in 1998.
"We have put the economic fundamentals in place... No one in his right mind would like to bring the Philippines back to that black pit of economic depression and non-performance," he added.
He said he was referring to the economy under late president Ferdinand Marcos, who was ousted in a 1986 popular revolt.
A constitutional provision barring Philippine presidents from seeking re-election has prompted speculation about the continuity of economic policies after Ramos.
It has also provoked moves among some Ramos' followers to push for amendments to the constitution to allow him to extend his term. Ramos has repeatedly denied he wants to stay on.

The Manila newspaper Today on Wednesday published a copy of what it said was a petition being passed around for signatures by Ramos supporters to demand constitutional changes and allow incumbent officials to stay in office until 2000.
It quoted a congressman as saying the petition had been signed by more than a million voters.
Asked if he would like to extend his term, Ramos said his main objective was to make sure that growth would continue beyond 1998.
"That is my wish, whoever sits in this chair here."
